newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia tries to toughen image in spat over Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Russia tries to toughen image in spat over Bosnia.

text.p: Russia has launched a diplomatic offensive against NATO swoops on suspected war criminals in Bosnia to try to toughen its image at home and abroad, Russian analysts said on Monday.

In the past four days, Moscow has condemned last Thursday's swoops as "cowboy raids", crossed swords over the issue with U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and told British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook the raids should not be repeated.

All-out diplomatic war appears unlikely. President Boris Yeltsin needs to concentrate on economic problems and does not want to upset steadily improving relations with the West. Moscow also has little leverage to influence policy on Bosnia.

But the Kremlin is using Bosnia -- which has not been a hot political issue in Moscow for months -- as a means of appeasing nationalist opponents and showing the West it is not a pushover, despite a recent deal with NATO, the independent analysts say.

"This is intended to show that Russia can express an independent view and that its position does not necessarily coincide with that of the West and NATO," said Andrei Kortunov, head of the Russian Science Foundation thinktank.

"I would not call it a serious dispute. No one wants that now -- especially the group that is in power. It is a diplomatic gesture indicating that Russia wants to reserve the right to express different views."
Yeltsin, 66, has signed several international agreements since returning to the Kremlin in February after long absences with heart problems and then pneumonia.
The agreements include a partnership deal signed with NATO leaders in May which gave Moscow a say, but not a veto, in some of the Western defence alliance's security matters.
That deal cleared the way for the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation to invite former Warsaw Pact members Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to join.
Nationalists and communists in the State Duma lower house of parliament accused Yeltsin of caving in by making the deal with NATO.

A tough foreign ministry statement last Friday denouncing the NATO action, followed by the objections expressed by Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov to Albright and Cook at talks in Moscow, were partly designed to respond to the Duma's criticism.
"Russia's reaction can clearly be seen as a ball thrown to the Duma," Kortunov said.

But there was no immediate need for such a gesture because the Duma is on its summer vacation and deputies' criticism of the government for doing too little to help fellow Orthodox Christian Serbs in ex-Yugoslavia have largely died down.
Russia may have genuine concerns over the NATO swoops, in which a police chief was shot dead after he resisted arrest and a hospital director was seized and extradited to The Hague.
Primakov told Albright Moscow feared the swoops could undermine Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic, who is backed by the West in a power struggle with former Serb leader Radovan Karadzic.

The Kremlin also fears a nationalist backlash in Moscow and an outbreak of violence in Bosnia if NATO tries to seize Karadzic and former Bosnian army commander Ratko Mladic, who are accused of war crimes.
"The message is that we have been forthcoming in relations with NATO but we will still stand firm on matters of national interest," said military and political analyst Dmitry Trenin.

"The message to the West is also that if you think the swoop in Bosnia was a test case for Karadzic and Mladic, you can think again. That (seizing them) could cause us problems at home and undermine what has been achieved in Bosnia."

Tensions between Russia and the West often flared over Bosnia during the 1992-1995 war but cooperation has improved since the Dayton peace treaty was signed. Western leaders have praised Russia's part in the international peacekeeping effort.

But one defence commentator said some of the Russian military wanted Moscow to withdraw its up to about 2,000 peacekeeping troops from Bosnia to cut costs as the government tries to pay off huge wage arrears to servicemen.
"What happens will depend on how vigorous NATO is in making follow-up raids. That would increase pressure for a pullout," Pavel Felgengauer, commentator for the Sevodnya newspaper, said.
